presenterNotes: The leap from two variables to three is mostly conceptual; the algebraic methods are the same. Emphasize pairing equations strategically.
Students often forget to back‑substitute into an original equation. Remind them that checking all three is the best way to catch errors.
The visual of planes intersecting helps ground the algebra. A physical model or 3D graphing tool can be very effective.
Real‑life problems motivate the topic. Have students create their own word problems and exchange with partners to solve.
title: Solving Linear Systems in Three Variables

blocks.title: Linear Equations in Three Variables

notes: $ a, b, c $ cannot all be zero.
Graph is a plane in 3D space.

formulaCard.title: Linear Equation in Three Variables
formulaCard.formula: $$ a x + b y + c z = d $$

explanation: A [[kw:linear equation in three variables]] is an equation of the form $ ax + by + cz = d $, where $ a $, $ b $, and $ c $ are not all zero. Its graph is a [[imp:plane]] in three‑dimensional space.
A [[kw:system of three linear equations]] consists of three such equations. A [[kw:solution]] is an [[imp:ordered triple]] $ (x, y, z) $ that makes all three equations true.

A system can have [[imp:exactly one solution]] (three planes intersect at a single point), [[imp:infinitely many solutions]] (planes intersect in a line or are the same plane), or [[imp:no solution]] (no common point).
A system with at least one solution is called [[kw:consistent]]. A system with no solution is [[kw:inconsistent]].

explanation: To solve a system of three equations in three variables algebraically, use the [[kw:elimination method]] (or substitution).
Step 1: [[imp:Pick a variable to eliminate]]. Pair the equations and eliminate that variable from two different pairs, creating two new equations in two variables.
Step 2: Solve the resulting two‑variable system for the two remaining unknowns.
Step 3: [[imp:Back‑substitute]] the values found into an original equation to find the third variable.
If you find a single ordered triple, the system has exactly one solution.

notes: Look for a variable with a coefficient of 1 or -1 if possible.
You can eliminate any variable; the answer will be the same.
Always check your solution in all three original equations.
formulaCard.title: Elimination Strategy
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{1. Choose a variable to eliminate.} $$ $$ \text{2. Combine two pairs of equations to get two equations in two variables.} $$ $$ \text{3. Solve the two‑variable system.} $$ $$ \text{4. Back‑substitute to find the third variable.} $$

formulaCard.title: Writing Solutions with a Parameter

explanation: During elimination, if you obtain a [[imp:false equation]] such as $ 0 = -7 $, the system has [[imp:no solution]]. It is inconsistent.
If you obtain an [[imp:identity]] such as $ 0 = 0 $, the system has [[imp:infinitely many solutions]]. It is consistent.

For infinitely many solutions, you can describe them using an ordered triple with a [[kw:parameter]]. For example, solve for two variables in terms of the third, and write the solution as $ (x, x+3, 0) $, where $ x $ can be any real number.
Graphically, no solution means the planes do not all intersect. Infinitely many means they intersect in a line or are identical.

explanation: Real‑world problems often involve three unknowns that satisfy three [[kw:constraints]].
Steps to model:
1. Identify the unknowns and assign variables.
2. Write a verbal model for each relationship (e.g., 'Section B = 3 × Section A').
3. Translate each verbal model into an equation.
4. Solve the resulting system using elimination or substitution.
5. Interpret the solution in the context of the problem.

formulaCard.title: Checklist for Three‑Variable Systems
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{1. Pair equations and eliminate one variable.} $$ $$ \text{2. Solve the resulting 2×2 system.} $$ $$ \text{3. Substitute back to find the third variable.} $$ $$ \text{4. Verify in all three original equations.} $$

explanation: **Understand**: We have three equations. We want to know if there is one solution, no solution, or infinitely many. Choose a variable to eliminate.
**Solve**: Pair equations, eliminate the chosen variable, solve the resulting two‑variable system, back‑substitute. Watch for false equations or identities.
**Conclude**: Write the solution as an ordered triple, or state 'no solution', or describe the infinite set using a parameter.

Example: $ 3x - 2y + z = 1 $, $ x + y - z = 4 $, $ 2x + 3y + 2z = 5 $. Eliminate $ z $ by adding Eq1 and Eq2 → $ 4x - y = 5 $. Add $ 2 \times $ Eq2 to Eq3 → $ 4x + 5y = 13 $. Solve the two: subtract to get $ -6y = -8 $ → $ y = 4/3 $, then $ x = 19/12 $, then $ z $ from Eq2. Solution: $ (19/12, 4/3, ...) $ — will be messy but exists.

confusionCorner.title: Fractions Are Okay!
confusionCorner.body: Solutions do not have to be integers. If you get fractions, keep them as fractions. They are exact; decimals may be approximations. [[imp:Don't round unless the problem asks you to.]]
